title: Terminal commands are interpreted as consisting of a command, options, arguments, and output.
body: A terminal is a window where developers issue text-based commands to a computer. What matters is not the black window itself, but the ability to understand the structure of the commands. For example, a command like `python script.py --check data.json` can be broken down into the program to be executed, the file being passed, the options, and the output. The command specifies what to run, the options modify how it runs, and the arguments pass target files or values. Just like reading code, commands are read from left to right. First, check if the first word is the actual program to be executed; next, see if there are any options; and finally, check which file or folder is the target. Since the same command can access completely different files depending on the current working directory, you should also check the path displayed at the prompt or the results of `pwd` or `Get-Location`. Distinguish between success messages, warnings, and errors in the output. A common mistake made by beginners is memorizing the entire command as a single block. If you do this, you won’t be able to adapt the command even if just the path changes. Furthermore, ignoring error messages and repeating the same command only obscures the root cause. You must first determine whether the error is due to a missing file, a lack of permissions, or the command itself not being found. In particular, PowerShell and Bash differ in line breaks, quotation marks, and path notation, so copying commands verbatim can lead to failure. When practicing, write commands in a four-column table: the executable, options, target arguments, and expected output. Then, identify where the actual output differs from what you expected. This habit extends to everything from running Python, checking Git status, installing packages, running a local server, to performing browser smoke tests. It’s best to view the terminal not as a scary window, but as a debugging tool for reading the status of your project.
when_to_show: When reading terminal commands, the CLI, and execution logs
detail: Instead of memorizing an entire terminal command, you should break it down into its executable, options, target arguments, and output to understand it. Even the same command can target different files depending on the current working directory. If an error occurs, it’s best to narrow down the cause step by step, starting with command syntax, then path, permissions, and finally the execution environment. Be sure to record the actual output as well.

title: Shell is a set of rules for interpreting commands, and PowerShell and Bash have different syntaxes.
body: A shell is a program that interprets commands entered by the user and passes them to the operating system. PowerShell, Bash, and zsh are all shells, but they differ in syntax and basic tools. PowerShell is commonly used on Windows, while Bash is frequently used on Ubuntu or Linux servers. Even within the same Python project, the line-breaking conventions, environment variable notation, path separators, and script activation commands vary depending on which shell is used to execute the commands. When reading PowerShell commands, look for verbs such as Set-Location, Get-Content, Test-Path, and Remove-Item. When reading Bash commands, short commands like `cd`, `ls`, `cat`, `grep`, `rm`, and `chmod` frequently appear. PowerShell often uses backticks when chaining commands, while Bash often uses backslashes. There are also differences in how environment variables are read—in PowerShell, it’s `$env:NAME`, while in Bash, it’s `$NAME`. Most mistakes occur when you copy and paste syntax from another shell verbatim. For example, pasting Bash’s `source .venv/bin/activate` into PowerShell won’t work, and pasting PowerShell’s `.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` into Ubuntu Bash won’t work either. To determine whether a command is incorrect or the Python code is incorrect, you must first check which shell you’re currently using. If an error occurs during the syntax check before execution, it may not be a Python issue. When practicing, write down your environment first before looking at the command. Note whether you’re using Windows PowerShell, WSL/Ubuntu Bash, or Git Bash. Then, you should be able to adjust the path notation and activation commands to match your environment. By doing this, you’ll be able to more reliably understand development documentation, server guides, GitHub Actions logs, and GPU server configuration commands.
when_to_show: When Looking at Differences Between PowerShell and Bash Commands, Line Breaks, and Path Notation Issues
detail: Since the shell defines the rules for interpreting commands, you should first check the syntax differences between PowerShell and Bash. Line breaks, paths, environment variables, and commands for activating virtual environments may differ. When a command fails, you need to determine whether the issue is a Python code error or a syntax error in the current shell.

title: Ubuntu and Linux are the foundation for server development commands.
body: Linux is a family of operating systems, and Ubuntu is a distribution that packages Linux in a user-friendly way. Even if developers work on a local Windows machine, they frequently encounter Ubuntu commands on servers, in Docker, on GitHub Actions, and on GPU workstations. Learning Ubuntu does not mean delving deeply into every operating system; rather, it means mastering the basic workflow of finding files on a server, installing packages, checking permissions, and running Python. When reading Ubuntu documentation, you’ll encounter terms such as bash commands, apt installation, sudo permissions, home directories, root directories, and file permissions. `pwd` is used to check the current directory, `ls` to list files, `cd` to navigate folders, `cat` to view file contents, and `chmod` to adjust execution permissions. Unlike paths in Windows, such as D:\projects, Linux uses paths separated by slashes, like /home/user/project. A common source of confusion for beginners is thinking that Ubuntu is a language like Python. Ubuntu is an environment for running code, while Python is a language that runs within that environment. Additionally, system packages installed via `apt` are different from Python packages installed via `pip`. For example, tools like `poppler` or `tesseract` may require installation via `apt`, while `pdfplumber` or `requests` may require installation via `pip`. When practicing, break down server commands into three layers: These are operating system commands, Python environment commands, and project execution commands. First, check how Ubuntu displays files and permissions; next, set up the Python environment using venv and pip; and finally, run the project script. Once you’ve established this distinction, you’ll be able to identify where a problem occurred more quickly when reviewing server setup logs.
when_to_show: When reading about Ubuntu/Linux server commands, WSL, and GPU server setup
detail: Ubuntu and Linux are operating system environments that execute code—they are not the Python language itself. When working with servers, Docker, and GPU hardware, you’ll frequently encounter concepts such as bash, apt, sudo, and file permissions. When reading commands, it’s helpful to divide them into three layers: operating system commands, Python environment commands, and project execution commands.

title: When dealing with path issues, you need to consider both the current working directory and the absolute/relative paths.
body: A path is an address that specifies the location of a file or folder. In a development environment, many errors are caused by differences in the execution location rather than by the code itself. An absolute path specifies the full location starting from the drive or root, while a relative path is determined relative to the current working directory. A path like `.\data\file.json` can point to different files depending on where PowerShell is currently located. When reading a command, first check the current working directory. In PowerShell, `Get-Location` displays the current location, while in Bash, `pwd` does the same. Next, use `Test-Path`, `ls`, or `Get-ChildItem` to verify that the relative path leads to the actual file from that location. In Python code, using `pathlib.Path` can minimize differences in path separators between Windows and Linux. Errors caused by failing to find a file usually stem from one of the following: the current location, filename, file extension, encoding, or permissions. Beginners often assume that a path string is always correct just because it looks right. However, running a script from a different folder can cause the same relative path to break. Paths containing spaces may be split into multiple arguments if not enclosed in quotes, and Windows backslashes can conflict with escape sequences in Python strings. Therefore, you must understand why you should use raw strings, slash conversion, or a combination of pathlib. When practicing, don’t just look at the path that caused the error; combine it with the base folder to construct the actual full path. Check if the file exists, and if it does, verify its read permissions and encoding. In automation scripts, start by navigating to the project root, and including the absolute path in the output makes debugging easier later on. With this topic, it’s more important to use it as a framework for narrowing down problem scenarios than simply memorizing commands. This card emphasizes that path issues require examining both the current working directory and absolute/relative paths together. This card guides you to check, in order, the current working directory, the relative path reference, and whether the file actually exists. If you record output messages and error codes according to the checklist “For path issues, examine the current working directory and both absolute and relative paths together,” they will serve as a reference point when reproducing the same situation.
when_to_show: When encountering FileNotFoundError, relative paths, and Set-Location issues
detail: The key to resolving path issues is determining where a relative path points relative to the current working directory. You can check the current location using PowerShell’s `Get-Location` or Bash’s `pwd` command, and then verify whether the file actually exists. In automation scripts, navigating to the project root and outputting the absolute path are extremely helpful for debugging.

title: Although `sudo` runs commands with administrative privileges, using it out of habit can be dangerous.
body: sudo is a tool in Ubuntu/Linux that allows you to run commands with administrative privileges. Since regular users cannot freely modify system-wide settings or protected folders, sudo is used only for necessary tasks. For example, installing system packages, restarting services, or modifying specific protected paths may require sudo. However, because of its powerful capabilities, using it incorrectly can corrupt system files or cause ownership issues in project folders. When you run a `sudo` command, it first asks why administrator privileges are needed. While `sudo apt install` is natural since it installs software on the system, you should exercise caution with commands like `sudo python script.py` or `sudo pip install`. If project files are created with root ownership, you may later encounter issues where you cannot modify them as a regular user. Even if you receive a “Permission denied” error, instead of immediately using `sudo`, you should first check which file or folder you were trying to access. A common mistake made by beginners is trying to resolve all permission errors with `sudo`. The actual cause might be that you’re in the wrong directory, a file is missing, or the virtual environment is set up incorrectly. Additionally, when running a command with `sudo`, your usual environment variables or `venv` settings may appear different. While administrative privileges can solve problems, they can also obscure the root cause. When practicing, break down your `sudo` commands into three parts: the reason administrator privileges are needed, the target being modified, and how to recover if the operation fails. By distinguishing whether you’re installing a package, modifying a system service, or changing file permissions, you can assess the risk level of the command. For developers, it’s more important to develop the habit of using `sudo` sparingly and accurately than to know a lot of commands.
when_to_show: When you see "sudo," "Permission denied," or commands requiring administrator privileges
detail: sudo is a tool intended only for tasks that require administrative privileges. If you immediately use sudo just because you get a “Permission denied” error, you may end up masking the root cause or causing file ownership issues. You should first identify which file or system setting you’re trying to change and narrow down whether the issue lies with the current folder, permissions, or the virtual environment.

title: apt and pip are used for different types of installations.
body: Although apt and pip both appear to be installation tools, they serve different purposes. apt is a tool for installing Ubuntu system packages, while pip is a tool for installing Python packages. For example, if `import requests` fails in your Python code, you may need to run `pip install requests`. Conversely, if external executable tools such as `pdfimages`, `tesseract`, or `poppler` are missing, you may need to install system packages using `apt install`. When reading a command, first determine whether you are trying to install a Python import target or an operating system executable. `pip install -r requirements.txt` is a command to install a list of Python packages, while `sudo apt install poppler-utils` is a command to install an external tool on Ubuntu. Remember that pip should be run within a virtual environment whenever possible to isolate project-specific dependencies, whereas apt affects the entire system. A common mistake made by beginners is trying to solve all installation problems with `pip`. While libraries that can be imported are handled by `pip`, tools executed via the command line or OS libraries may be handled by `apt`. Conversely, if you try to install a Python package using `sudo apt`, an outdated version may be installed, or it may not be linked to your project’s venv. Since `sudo pip install` can further complicate your environment, it’s generally safer to avoid it. When practicing, look for clues in error messages. A `ModuleNotFoundError` is likely related to a Python package, while “command not found” is likely related to a system command. After installation, use the `which` command or `python -m pip --version` to verify which environment the package was actually installed in. Distinguishing between apt and pip significantly reduces trial and error when setting up servers, installing PDF/OCR tools, and building a FastAPI runtime environment.
when_to_show: When comparing `apt install` and `pip install`
detail: Although both apt and pip look like installation commands, they are used for different purposes. apt installs Ubuntu system packages or third-party executables, while pip installs packages required for Python imports. You should determine which layer the installation issue lies in by checking the type of error—whether it’s a `ModuleNotFoundError` or a “command not found” error.

title: chmod and file permissions determine who can read and execute a file
body: chmod is a command used to change file permissions in Linux/Ubuntu. File permissions determine who can read, write, or execute a file. If you have a script file and receive a “Permission denied” error when trying to run it, you may not have execute permissions. In such cases, you can add execute permissions using a command like `chmod +x script.sh`. Since file permissions represent a balance between security and convenience, granting them indiscriminately can be risky. When checking permissions, look at the user, group, and others categories. In the `ls -l` output, `r` stands for read, `w` for write, and `x` for execute. Python files can usually be run using the interpreter (e.g., `python script.py`) even if the file itself lacks execute permissions. On the other hand, if you want to run the file directly (e.g., `./run.sh`), execute permissions are required. When using the `chmod` command, it is most important to verify the target file and the specific permissions you are changing. Beginners may be tempted to simply copy commands like `chmod 777`, which grants all permissions, but this is not secure. Rather than rushing through the task, you should determine whether the actual permissions needed are read, write, or execute. Also, since the issue might not be related to permissions—but rather a wrong current directory or a different filename—always verify the current directory and filename using `ls`, `pwd`, or `Test-Path` before running `chmod`. When practicing, create a table listing the current permissions of the file causing the error, how it was executed, and the minimum permissions required. When deploying to a server or writing automation scripts, it’s important to get into the habit of not granting excessive permissions and limiting access only to necessary users. Understanding permissions helps reduce mistakes—such as tangling project file ownership—that can occur when mixing `sudo` and `chmod`. It’s important to use this topic as a framework for narrowing down problem scenarios rather than simply memorizing commands. This card explains that `chmod` and file permissions determine who can read and execute a file. This card separates and verifies file permissions, execution methods, and the minimum required permissions. If you record output messages and error codes according to the checklist in “chmod and file permissions determine who can read and execute a file,” they will serve as a reference point when reproducing the same situation.
when_to_show: When you see "chmod +x," "execution permission," or "Permission denied"
detail: chmod is a command that changes who can read, write, and execute a file. If you receive a “Permission denied” error, rather than simply granting full permissions with a command like `chmod 777`, you should verify whether the actual permission required is read or execute. It’s important to get into the habit of analyzing the file’s location, how it’s executed, the current user, and the minimum necessary permissions.

title: venv is a Python toolbox used separately for each project.
body: venv does not copy the operating system; it isolates a project-specific Python path and site-packages. Activation is a PATH convenience, and an explicit environment interpreter works without it. Pins and tests are also needed for stronger reproducibility.
when_to_show: When reviewing venv, virtual_environment, python, dependency
detail: venv does not copy the operating system; it isolates a project-specific Python path and site-packages. Activation is a PATH convenience, and an explicit environment interpreter works without it. Pins and tests are also needed for stronger reproducibility.

title: "activate" and "deactivate" change which Python environment the current terminal is using.
body: Activation changes the current shell's PATH so the environment's Python is preferred; deactivation reverses that change. Activation is optional because the environment interpreter can be invoked directly. Verify the real path with sys.executable and python -m pip --version rather than trusting only the prompt label.

Activation is optional because the environment interpreter can be invoked directly. Verify the real path with sys.executable and python -m pip --version rather than trusting only the prompt label.

title: `python -m pip` ensures that the pip currently associated with Python is used.
body: "python -m pip" means to run the pip module using the currently running Python. If you simply use "pip install," which version of pip is used may depend on the PATH settings in your shell. In particular, if you have multiple Python installations on Windows, or if you repeatedly activate and deactivate venv, pip and Python may point to different environments. In this case, using a command like `python -m pip install requests` ensures that pip from the same environment as the current Python is used. When interpreting the command, the installation location is checked before the target to be installed. `python -m pip --version` shows not only the pip version but also which Python path pip is linked to. If a venv is active, it’s natural for that path to appear inside the `.venv` directory. When an `import` error occurs, you should check the Python path, the pip path, the current working directory, and the virtual environment status before reinstalling the package. A common mistake made by beginners is assuming that since they’ve already run `pip install`, the import will definitely work. If the Python interpreter actually being used is from a different environment, it won’t be able to access the installed package. Additionally, Jupyter, VS Code, and the terminal may use different interpreters. Therefore, it’s important to get into the habit of verifying that you’re definitely using the pip from your current Python environment. When practicing, run `where python`, `where pip`, and `python -m pip --version` as a set. On Ubuntu, use `which python` and `which pip`. Then, verify that the import actually works by running `python -c "import package_name"`. Once you master this routine, you’ll be able to narrow down package installation issues based on concrete evidence rather than relying on intuition.
when_to_show: When imports fail due to differences between the pip and Python environments

If you’ve installed a module but can’t import it, you should check the Python path, the pip path, and whether the venv is active.

body: ModuleNotFoundError means Python could not resolve an import name. Causes include an environment mismatch, a typo, launch location, package structure, or a local file shadowing another module. Check sys.executable, python -m pip show, the import path, and filenames in order.

title: Git manages the working directory, staging area, commits, and remote repositories separately.
body: Git is a tool for managing the history of file changes. Beginners often think of Git as something like a "Save" button, but in reality, it consists of distinct components: the working directory, the staging area, commits, and remote repositories. The working directory contains the current state of the files you’re editing, while the staging area is where you select changes to include in your next commit. A commit is the action of saving the selected changes as a single record, and “remote” refers to a remote repository like GitHub. When reading Git commands, you should check which stage your changes are currently in. `git status` shows the status of the working directory and the staging area, while `git diff` displays the actual lines of changes that haven’t been committed yet. `git add` adds changes to the list of candidates for the next commit, and `git commit` saves those candidates as a commit. `git push` is the step that sends the local commit to the remote repository. You need to distinguish between these stages to avoid overlooking changes that have been committed but not yet pushed. A common mistake beginners make is thinking that `git add` uploads changes to the remote repository, or assuming that simply committing a change means it’s been pushed to GitHub. Also, if you add all modified files at once, temporary files or debug output may get mixed in. That’s why it’s important to get into the habit of checking `git status` and `git diff` to select only the necessary files. When practicing, modify a single file and observe how the status changes by running the commands in the following order: `git status`, `git diff`, `git add`, `git status`, `git commit`, `git log`, and `git push`. Once you’ve internalized this model, it becomes much easier to connect the dots to subsequent concepts like tags, branches, merges, and restores. Git is a tool for understanding where changes are located, rather than simply memorizing commands. It’s important to use this topic as a framework for narrowing down problem scenarios rather than simply memorizing commands. This card explains that Git manages the working directory, staging area, commits, and remote repository separately. This card distinguishes the stages handled by each of these components: the working directory, staging area, commits, and remote repository. If you record output messages and error codes according to the checklist for “Git manages the working directory, staging area, commits, and remote repository,” they will serve as a reference point when you need to reproduce the same situation.

The `git add` command is not an upload to a remote repository; rather, it is the step of selecting changes to include in the next commit. Similarly, a `commit` does not yet reflect the changes on GitHub. You should use `status` and `diff` to review where changes have been made, and understand the `commit` and `push` steps as distinct processes.

title: "status," "diff," "add," and "commit" are the basic steps for safely creating a commit.
body: `status`, `diff`, `add`, and `commit` are Git’s most basic workflows. `git status` shows which files have changed, and `git diff` shows exactly which lines have been added or deleted. `git add` selects the changes to include in the next commit, and `git commit` saves that set of changes as a commit. Following this sequence helps minimize the risk of accidentally committing temporary files or unintended changes. After modifying the code, first run a validation command, then use `git status --short` to view the list of modified files. After confirming that only the expected files have been modified, use `git diff --stat` to assess the scope of the changes, and check the file-by-file diff if necessary. If the changes are correct, use `git add` to stage only the necessary files. Write a short and specific commit message so that you can understand what you did just by looking at the log later. Common mistakes made by beginners include committing before verifying or using `git add all` without checking `git status`. In particular, temporary files created by automation scripts may remain untracked. If such files are committed, the repository becomes cluttered, making it difficult to identify the cause of issues in subsequent work. If you don’t check the diff, you might think you only need to update the version string but overlook significant changes to data files. When practicing, stick to a fixed pre-commit checklist: pass validation, check `status`, review the diff, add only the necessary files, then commit, tag, and push. This routine serves as a quality gate not only for small learning apps but also for production code. Think of it not as memorizing Git commands, but as a procedure for creating safe units of change. It’s important to use this topic as a framework for narrowing down problem scenarios rather than simply memorizing commands. On this card, `status`, `diff`, `add`, and `commit` are the basic routine for creating a safe commit. On this card, you use `status` to check file status, verify actual line changes with `diff`, and then define the scope for `add` and `commit`. If you record the output messages and error codes in the order of the “basic routine for creating a safe commit” (status, diff, add, commit), they will serve as a reference point when you need to reproduce the same situation.
when_to_show: When reviewing git_status, git_diff, git_add, git_commit
detail: `status`, `diff`, `add`, and `commit` are the basic steps for making a safe commit. Use `status` to view the modified files, use `diff` to verify the actual line changes, and then add only the necessary files before committing. Committing before verification or including temporary files such as `.tmp` makes it difficult to trace the cause of issues later on.

title: "tag," "push," and "pull" are commands used to synchronize the local repository with a remote reference.
body: A tag is a label attached to a specific commit. If you apply a tag when a feature has stabilized or at a deployment milestone, it makes it easy to revisit that state later. `push` is a command that sends local commits or tags to a remote repository, while `pull` is a command that fetches remote changes and merges them into the local repository. `origin` is typically the default remote repository name, and `origin/main` refers to the state of the remote `main` branch. When reading commands, you must distinguish whether a commit exists only locally or has also been pushed to the remote repository. Even after running `git commit`, the changes are not yet reflected on GitHub. You must run a `push` command, such as `git push origin main --tags`, to push both the remote `main` branch and the tag. Conversely, to continue working on another device, you must use `pull` or `clone` to fetch the remote state. `tag --points-at HEAD` is useful for checking which tag is attached to the current commit. A common point of confusion for beginners is the difference between tags and branches. A branch is a constantly evolving workflow, while a tag is typically a label that points to a specific, fixed commit. Also, since tags aren’t always pushed automatically, you may need to use the `--tags` option. Commits that haven’t been pushed to the remote repository may exist on your computer but won’t be visible on other PCs or on GitHub Pages. When practicing, create a commit, check the hash in the log, apply a tag, verify it with `tag --points-at HEAD`, and then push. After pushing, check the log to confirm that `origin/main` points to the same commit. Understanding this process allows you to leave a safe recovery point after each successful verification.
when_to_show: When viewing tag creation, the origin/main branch, and the push/pull workflow
detail: A tag is a label that pins a specific commit so it can be easily found later, and `push` is a command that uploads the local history to a remote repository. Simply making a commit does not automatically update GitHub or Pages. To ensure a stable baseline, you must also verify the difference between tags and branches, the location of `origin/main`, and whether the `--tags` option was used during the `push` command.

title: "branch," "conflict," and "restore" are ways to split and revert changes.
body: A branch is a Git feature that creates a separate workflow from the main branch. Major experiments or risky changes can be carried out on a new branch and merged into the main branch after validation. A merge is the action of combining changes from another branch into the current branch. If different people have made conflicting changes to the same part of the same file, a conflict occurs. Since Git cannot automatically resolve this, a user must review the conflict indicators and choose which changes to keep. Undo commands have different scopes. `restore` is typically used to revert changes to working files that have not yet been committed. `reset` can alter the commit history or the staging area, so it requires greater caution. `revert` creates a new commit that undoes changes that have already been committed, so it is often safer when working with a shared history. Before using any command, you must verify whether the changes are pre-commit or post-commit, and whether they have been pushed to the remote repository. A common pitfall for beginners is lumping `restore`, `reset`, and `revert` together as mere “recovery” commands. You could lose uncommitted work, and forcibly altering a shared history can cause problems in collaboration. Committing without removing conflict markers can break your code, so you must also check for remaining <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers. When practicing, create a branch to modify a small file, then use `diff` to compare it with the `main` branch. If a conflict arises, choose which changes to keep, verify them, and then commit. To undo changes, first review the status and log before making a decision. While Git is a tool designed to prevent mistakes, the undo command can be used safely only when you fully understand the current state. It is more important to use this topic as a framework for narrowing down problem scenarios rather than simply memorizing commands. This card explains that branches, conflicts, and restores are methods for isolating and reverting changes. In this card, we examine the flow of changes split across branches, conflict markers, and the scope of risk associated with the restore command separately. If you record the output messages and error codes in the order specified in “Branches, Conflicts, and Restore: Methods for Isolating and Reverting Changes,” they will serve as a reference point when you need to reproduce the same situation.

detail: A "branch" divides the workflow, and a "conflict" refers to a clash of changes that Git was unable to automatically resolve. While "restore," "reset," and "revert" all seem to mean "undo," their scope of impact differs. To use them safely, you should first check whether the changes were made before or after a commit, whether they were pushed to the remote repository, and whether any conflict markers remain.

title: Environment variables and .env files inject configurations and secrets from outside the code.
body: Environment variables are configuration values injected from outside the code. It is safer not to hardcode values that vary by environment—such as API keys, database addresses, execution modes, and model paths—directly into the code. A .env file is used to store these values separately during local development, and Python code can read them using `os.getenv` or the `dotenv` library. It is crucial not to upload actual sensitive values to public repositories. When reviewing code, trace where configuration values come from. Values retrieved by name—such as `os.getenv('API_KEY')`—may not reveal the actual value within the code. You should also check whether the code uses a default value when the value is missing, throws an error immediately, or displays a specific message. The .env file is usually added to .gitignore, and instead, a sample file like .env.example—which only shows the names—is shared. A common mistake made by beginners is hard-coding an API key as a string directly into the code and uploading it to GitHub. If this happens, others could use the service with your account or incur charges. Additionally, if you assume the issue is solely a code problem when the environment variable isn’t set, it becomes difficult to identify the root cause. In deployment environments, server configurations or secret settings on the hosting platform are often used instead of the local `.env` file. When practicing, write down the environment variable name, storage location, loading code, and behavior when missing in four separate columns. Then, distinguish between values that should not be committed to Git and example values that can be committed. Understanding environment variables allows you to view security, deployment, local development, and API integration as a single, cohesive process. It’s important to use this topic as a framework for narrowing down problem scenarios rather than simply memorizing commands. On this card, note that environment variables and the .env file inject settings and secrets from outside the code. On this card, check the environment variable name, storage location, loading code, and whether it’s exposed in Git, in that order. If you record output messages and error codes according to the checklist for “Environment variables and .env files inject settings and secrets from outside the code,” they will serve as a reference point when reproducing the same situation.
when_to_show: When viewing API keys, .env, os.getenv, and environment settings
detail: Environment variables and .env files are ways to inject values that vary by environment—such as API keys, database addresses, and execution modes—from outside the code. It’s safer to share only example files on GitHub rather than the actual secret values. When reviewing code, check the variable names, where they’re loaded from, what happens if they’re missing, and whether they’re exposed on Git.

title: GPU, NVIDIA driver, CUDA, and PyTorch CUDA build are different layers.
body: Separate GPU hardware, the NVIDIA driver, the PyTorch build in the selected environment, and its compatible CUDA runtime. PyTorch wheels can bundle required runtime components, so a system CUDA toolkit is not always required. Compare nvidia-smi, torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.version.cuda, and sys.executable.
when_to_show: When looking at CUDA installation, GPU servers, and the PyTorch runtime environment
detail: Separate GPU hardware, the NVIDIA driver, the PyTorch build in the selected environment, and its compatible CUDA runtime. PyTorch wheels can bundle required runtime components, so a system CUDA toolkit is not always required. Compare nvidia-smi, torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.version.cuda, and sys.executable.

title: `torch.cuda.is_available` checks whether PyTorch can actually use the GPU.
body: `torch.cuda.is_available()` is a function that checks whether PyTorch in the current Python environment can use a CUDA GPU. If this value is `True`, it means that PyTorch can use a CUDA device; if it is `False`, the code will run on the CPU, or you will need to review your environment settings. In AI code, it is common to use a pattern like `device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'` to use the GPU if available, and fall back to the CPU if not. When reading code, verify that the model and tensors are on the same device. `model.to(device)` moves the model parameters to the CPU or GPU, while `tensor.to(device)` moves the input data to the same device. If the model is on the GPU but the input tensor is on the CPU, a device mismatch error may occur. Using the GPU doesn’t simply mean the hardware is present; it means the model and data have been loaded onto the correct device. A common source of confusion for beginners is assuming that the CUDA check code resolves all installation issues. If `is_available` returns `False`, you need to narrow down the cause further. Check whether the NVIDIA driver is missing, if you’re using a CPU-only version of PyTorch, if the venv is different, if the remote server lacks a GPU, or if the device is hidden by `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`. Furthermore, even if `is_available` returns `True`, a “CUDA out of memory” error may occur during execution if there is insufficient VRAM. When practicing, try printing `torch.cuda.is_available()`, `torch.version.cuda`, and `torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)` together. Next, try moving a small tensor to CUDA and performing a calculation to more clearly determine whether actual computation is possible. This routine is fundamental for checking the environment for LoRA, embeddings, image processing, and model inference.
when_to_show: When looking at the code for checking PyTorch CUDA and selecting a device
detail: `torch.cuda.is_available` is a function that checks whether PyTorch in the current Python environment can use CUDA devices. Even if it returns `True`, an error may occur if the model and tensor are not loaded onto the same device. If the result is `False`, you should investigate possible causes, such as the absence of a GPU, driver issues, a CPU-only version of PyTorch, or a different virtual environment (`venv`).

title: nvidia-smi is a basic diagnostic tool for checking GPU usage and VRAM status.
body: `nvidia-smi` is the primary command for checking the status of an NVIDIA GPU. This command displays the GPU name, driver version, CUDA compatibility information, GPU utilization, VRAM usage, and running processes. When AI tasks are running slowly, you can quickly check whether the GPU is actually being used, if memory is already full, or if another process is monopolizing the GPU. When reviewing the output, look at the “GPU util” and “memory usage” metrics. A low “GPU util” value does not necessarily mean the GPU is performing poorly. The GPU may be waiting due to data loading, CPU preprocessing, or disk I/O. If VRAM usage is high, the causes could include model size, batch size, input length, dtype, or the number of concurrent executions. If you encounter a “CUDA out of memory” error, you may need to reduce the batch size, shorten the input length, or use a smaller model. A common mistake made by beginners is assuming that all problems are solved just by looking at a single line of `nvidia-smi` output. nvidia-smi shows the system’s GPU status, but to determine whether your Python code is using that GPU properly, you need to check `torch.cuda` and verify the device assignment in your code. Also, even if `util` is 0%, the model might still be loading or undergoing CPU preprocessing, so you should review the logs and monitor the elapsed time. When practicing, compare the `nvidia-smi` output before and during model execution. Record which processes are using GPU memory, how much VRAM is remaining, and how memory usage changes when you adjust the batch size. Rather than relying on intuition, GPU issues can be reliably resolved by analyzing the hardware status, Python environment, and code flow together.
when_to_show: When you see "GPU usage," "VRAM shortage," or "CUDA out of memory"
detail: nvidia-smi is a basic diagnostic tool that displays the GPU name, driver version, utilization, VRAM usage, and running processes. Low GPU utilization does not always indicate a GPU issue; it could be due to waiting for data to load or CPU preprocessing. VRAM shortages should be evaluated in conjunction with batch size, model size, and input length.

title: A virtual environment is a project-specific Python toolbox.
body: A virtual environment is not a way to install Python anew, but rather a method for isolating the package space used by a single project. For example, Project A can use NumPy 1.x, while Project B can use NumPy 2.x. If you mix the two in a single global environment, it becomes confusing later on to determine which project depends on which version. That’s why you typically create a .venv file inside the project folder and activate it only within that terminal. The key is to isolate “the Python environment used by this project,” rather than “the Python environment for the entire computer.”
detail: It’s easy to think of a virtual environment as a project-specific Python toolbox. Rather than changing the Python installation on the entire computer, it isolates a separate space for the packages used by a specific project. This helps reduce conflicts when multiple projects require different library versions and makes it easy to recreate the same environment later.

title: The reason for using a virtual environment is to reduce conflicts and ensure reproducibility.
body: The main reason for using a virtual environment is to minimize package conflicts, since the required libraries and versions can vary from project to project. Another reason is reproducibility. If you save the environment you’ve created in a `requirements.txt` file, you can recreate a similar environment later on another PC or server. As a beginner, you might wonder, “Why make things so complicated?” but as soon as you have two or more projects, a virtual environment becomes a safety net that helps reduce mistakes.
detail: The reason for using a virtual environment is to minimize package conflicts and ensure a reproducible runtime environment. While this may seem like a hassle when you’re working on a single project, as the number of projects increases, it becomes difficult to trace which global installation caused a code failure. When used in conjunction with `requirements.txt`, it makes it easy to recreate the environment on a new PC or server.

title: You must use pip after running `activate` for the installation to take effect in that environment.
body: Activation makes python prefer the environment interpreter, which is convenient for installation and execution. It is not required; the environment's Python can be invoked directly. Use python -m pip and sys.executable to confirm that installation and execution target the same interpreter.
detail: Activation makes python prefer the environment interpreter, which is convenient for installation and execution. It is not required; the environment's Python can be invoked directly. Use python -m pip and sys.executable to confirm that installation and execution target the same interpreter.

title: requirements.txt is a notepad for recreating the installation list.
body: requirements.txt is a list of packages required for a project. Typically, you can generate it by running `pip freeze > requirements.txt` to save the list of installed packages in the current environment, or you can manually list only the essential packages. On another computer, you can recreate a similar environment by running `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`. It’s important to note that while `requirements.txt` isn’t code itself, it serves as a checklist of what’s needed to run the code. That’s why it’s often included alongside the code when uploading it to GitHub.
detail: requirements.txt is a file that lists the packages required to run the project. Although it is not code itself, it serves as a checklist for setting up the environment to run the code, so it is often included in the repository. In a new environment, run `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt` to install the packages. Don’t just check for a successful installation message; you must also verify that the code actually runs.

title: Ubuntu and WSL can serve as a way to practice Linux commands.
body: Ubuntu is a Linux distribution that frequently appears in documentation on server development and AI development. WSL is a feature that allows you to run a Linux environment within Windows. In Windows, you often use PowerShell commands, while in Ubuntu/WSL, you typically use bash commands. Even for a simple task like navigating to a different folder, the syntax differs—PowerShell uses `Set-Location`, while bash uses `cd`. Therefore, when reviewing commands, you should first check which shell you are currently using.
detail: Ubuntu is a Linux distribution frequently mentioned in server development documentation, and WSL is a feature that allows you to practice using a Linux environment within Windows. Since PowerShell and Bash have different command syntaxes, you must verify which environment a copied command is intended for. It’s important to get into the habit of checking your current shell and path notation first.

title: sudo requests administrator privileges, but it is not a one-size-fits-all solution.
body: In Linux, `sudo` means to run a command with administrative privileges. It may be necessary when installing system packages, such as with `apt install`. However, it’s risky to always use `sudo` just because you get a “Permission denied” error. This is because the issue could stem from an incorrect file path, a faulty virtual environment, or a lack of execution permissions. In particular, habitually using `sudo` with `pip install` can cause packages to get mixed in with the system Python, which can lead to further complications with your environment later on.
detail: "sudo" means running a command with administrative privileges; it is not a magic button that fixes every error. If you see a "Permission denied" error, you should first check the file location, execution permissions, ownership, and any issues with the virtual environment. In particular, be careful when using `sudo pip install`, as it can mess up your system Python.

title: To troubleshoot CUDA issues, check the GPU, drivers, and PyTorch build separately
body: When a GPU isn’t detected during AI development, don’t focus on just one possible cause. First, use `nvidia-smi` to verify that the GPU and drivers are recognized. Next, check in PyTorch to see if `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns `True`. Even if a GPU is present, you may not be able to use it in your Python code if the drivers, CUDA runtime, or PyTorch CUDA build are incompatible. A “CUDA out of memory” error is often caused by insufficient VRAM rather than an installation issue, so the recommended approach is to reduce the batch size.
detail: If you encounter a CUDA issue, you should check the GPU hardware, NVIDIA driver, CUDA runtime, and PyTorch CUDA build separately. While `nvidia-smi` displays the hardware and driver status, you must use `torch.cuda.is_available` to verify whether your Python code is actually using the GPU. An OOM error is more likely caused by insufficient VRAM than by an installation issue.

title: Start by learning the Git workflow: status → add → commit → push
body: When you’re first learning Git, you don’t need to memorize all the commands at once. Start by using `git status` to check your current changes, then use `git add` to select the files you want to include in the commit, and finally use `git commit` to create a local commit. To push changes to a remote repository like GitHub, use `git push`. `git diff` is a command that lets you check what has changed before committing. The key point is that “modifying files,” “committing changes,” and “pushing to a remote repository” are distinct steps.
detail: The basic Git workflow involves checking the status to review changes, using `add` to select files to commit, creating a local commit with `commit`, and then pushing the changes to the remote repository with `push`. Modifying files, saving changes, and pushing them to the remote repository are distinct steps. Checking the diff before committing can help minimize unintended changes.
